The Standard Revenue Case: How to Recognize, Record, and Disclose Typical Sales Transactions

Summary
This note explains a canonical “standard” revenue scenario under ASC 606 / IFRS 15: a single performance obligation, control transfers at a point in time (sale of goods), consideration fixed or determinable, no significant financing component, and no variable consideration. It includes the 5‑step recognition recap, clear journal entries (cash and credit sales), a worked numeric example, common pitfalls, disclosure requirements, and a short preparer checklist.

1. What is the “standard” revenue case?
- Characteristics: single performance obligation (one SKU or product line), transfer of control at a point in time (physical delivery and legal title or other indicators), consideration is fixed/determinable, no significant financing component (short credit terms, e.g., net 30), no variable consideration (no rebates, returns not expected materially), and contract costs are routine.
- Why it’s simple: Under ASC 606 / IFRS 15, point‑in‑time transfer with no variables means revenue is recognized when control transfers — usually at delivery or shipment (depending on contract terms).

Key terms (brief):
- Performance obligation: a promise to transfer a distinct good or service to a customer.
- Transfer of control: customer obtains the ability to direct use of and obtain substantially all remaining benefits from the good.

2. 5‑step model recap (why the standard case maps neatly)
1) Identify the contract: enforceable agreement with commercial substance.
2) Identify performance obligations: here, a single obligation to deliver goods.
3) Determine transaction price: fixed amount payable by customer.
4) Allocate price to obligations: entire price to the single obligation.
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) performance obligation is satisfied: at the point in time when control transfers (delivery/transfer of title).

Because there’s a single obligation and fixed price, steps 3–4 are straightforward and revenue recognition occurs at a single point in time.

3. Typical journal entries
A. Cash sale (point in time):
- At point of sale/delivery:
  Dr Cash  XX
  Cr Revenue  XX
  Dr Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)  YY
  Cr Inventory  YY

B. Credit sale (point in time):
- At point of sale/delivery:
  Dr Accounts Receivable  XX
  Cr Revenue  XX
  Dr Cost of Goods Sold (COGS)  YY
  Cr Inventory  YY
- When cash collected:
  Dr Cash  XX
  Cr Accounts Receivable  XX

C. If sales tax is collected (presentation note):
- Collecting sales tax (US GAAP typical presentation):
  Dr Accounts Receivable / Cash  (XX + tax)
  Cr Revenue  XX
  Cr Sales Tax Payable  (tax)
- Note: Under ASC 606/IFRS 15 revenue should exclude amounts collected on behalf of taxing authorities; present sales tax as liability unless taxes are included in the transaction price in your jurisdiction.

4. Worked numeric example (single transaction)
Facts: Goods sold for $10,000 (invoice), cost $6,000. Sold on credit, terms net 30. No returns/discounts. No significant financing component.

Journal entries:
- On date of sale/delivery (point in time):
  Dr Accounts Receivable 10,000
  Cr Revenue 10,000
  Dr Cost of Goods Sold 6,000
  Cr Inventory 6,000

- On cash collection (30 days later):
  Dr Cash 10,000
  Cr Accounts Receivable 10,000

Financial statement effects (period of sale):
- Income statement: Revenue 10,000; COGS 6,000; Gross profit 4,000 (operating/income tax effects as applicable).
- Balance sheet (immediately after sale): Accounts receivable increases by 10,000; inventory decreases by 6,000; net working capital increases by 4,000 (which ultimately flows to retained earnings through profit).

5. Disclosures (what preparers typically disclose under ASC 606 / IFRS 15)
- Revenue disaggregation: by major product lines and/or geography, if material.
- Timing of revenue recognition: point‑in‑time (goods transferred at delivery).
- Significant judgments: e.g., determination of transfer of control, assessment of collectibility (if any doubt), or estimates of returns/allowances.
- Contract balances: opening and closing balances of accounts receivable, contract assets, and contract liabilities (deferred revenue), and changes during the period.
- Remaining performance obligations: usually not material for simple, completed sales; disclose if material.
- Policy disclosure: revenue recognition policy, presentation of sales taxes, and classification of costs associated with obtaining/fulfilling contracts if material.

Presentation notes: Under US GAAP, sales taxes collected are excluded from revenue and shown as a liability. IFRS follows the same principle. Disaggregation format can be a table by product line and region per period.

6. Common pitfalls and cautions
- Point-in-time vs. over-time: don’t assume point-in-time automatically — check indicators such as continuous transfer, customer control during production, or seller’s obligation to rework goods.
- Significant financing component: long payment terms (months/years) may require adjusting transaction price for the time value of money; short terms (net 30) typically do not.
- Sales taxes and similar items: include only the consideration to which the entity expects to be entitled; exclude taxes collected on behalf of third parties.
- Collectibility: at contract inception assess whether it is probable the entity will collect the consideration; if not, account for the contract differently (e.g., as a deposit or recognize revenue only to extent probable).
- Returns and variable consideration: if returns/allowances are possible, estimate and constrain variable amounts per ASC 606/IFRS 15.
- Presentation mistakes: misclassifying contract balances or failing to disclose significant judgments.

7. Tax and audit considerations (brief)
- Taxation: revenue recognition for financial reporting under ASC 606/IFRS 15 does not automatically determine tax timing — consult tax rules/jurisdictional guidance.
- Audit focus areas: collectibility, cut‑off around period end (ship vs. bill vs. deliver), completeness of sales, accuracy of COGS and inventory movement, and adequacy of disclosures.

8. Preparer checklist (quick, use before closing)
- Confirm contract terms: price, delivery terms, who bears shipping risk, and when title transfers.
- Confirm single vs. multiple performance obligations.
- Verify transaction price is fixed/determinable and assess collectibility.
- Determine whether the timing of transfer is point‑in‑time or over‑time (document indicators).
- Check for sales taxes/withholdings and present accordingly.
- Ensure inventory reduction and COGS entries match physical and perpetual records.
- Review contract balances (AR / deferred revenue) and reconcile to ledger.
- Confirm disclosures: policy, disaggregation, contract balances, and significant judgments.

References
- FASB ASC 606, Revenue from Contracts with Customers; IFRS 15, Revenue from Contracts with Customers.
- Big Four practice guides and AICPA illustrative disclosures (PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG summaries and checklists).
- PCAOB/AICPA staff observations on common revenue recognition issues.

Editor compliance notes (for your review)
- Please confirm ASC 606 / IFRS 15 references are accurate and that journal entries and sales tax presentation are consistent with US GAAP practice; note any jurisdictional differences where relevant. Ensure checklist items are practical and not prescriptive.

(End of draft)

Title: The Standard‑Revenue Case — Practical Guide to ASC 606 / IFRS 15 for SaaS and Subscription Contracts

Executive summary
The “standard‑revenue case” describes the typical workflow for recognizing revenue under ASC 606 / IFRS 15: identify the contract, define performance obligations, determine and allocate the transaction price, and recognize revenue as obligations are satisfied. This guide gives finance teams a practical, example‑driven walkthrough (including journal entries), common pitfalls, and a short checklist to help apply the model to a typical SaaS subscription plus one‑time services.

Quick overview: the five‑step model (concise)
1. Identify the contract with a customer — a legally enforceable agreement creating rights and obligations.
2. Identify the performance obligations — promises to transfer distinct goods or services.
3. Determine the transaction price — the amount expected to be entitled to, including variable consideration (constrained by the reversal risk).
4. Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations — typically by standalone selling price (SSP).
5. Recognize revenue when (or as) performance obligations are satisfied — at a point in time or over time.

Definitions (one‑liners)
- Standalone selling price (SSP): the price at which an entity would sell a good or service separately to a customer.
- Variable consideration: contract consideration that varies (credits, discounts, incentives); recorded only to the extent it’s not likely to reverse materially.
- Satisfied over time: revenue recognized progressively as control transfers (e.g., subscriptions delivered over time).

Standard walkthrough: SaaS subscription + one‑time implementation (numeric example)
Scenario specifics (required numbers):
- Contract term: 12 months.
- Subscription fee: $120,000 (billed and collected annually at contract inception).
- One‑time implementation service fee: $10,000 (performed at contract start).
- Standalone selling prices: SaaS subscription $120,000; implementation $10,000 (i.e., SSPs equal list prices).

Step A — Determine transaction price and allocate
- Total transaction price = $120,000 (SaaS) + $10,000 (implementation) = $130,000.
- Because SSPs equal list prices, allocation is straightforward: $120,000 to SaaS; $10,000 to implementation.

Step B — Timing of recognition
- Implementation: performed at inception (point in time) → recognize $10,000 immediately.
- SaaS: delivered over the 12‑month term (satisfied over time) → recognize $120,000 ratably over 12 months = $10,000 per month.

Journal entries (illustrative):
1) At contract inception (cash collected annually):
- Dr Cash $130,000
- Cr Deferred revenue — SaaS $120,000
- Cr Revenue — Implementation $10,000
(Explanation: Implementation performed at contract start is recognized immediately; SaaS portion is deferred.)

2) Monthly revenue recognition for months 1–12 (start of each month or end, per policy):
- Dr Deferred revenue — SaaS $10,000
- Cr Revenue — SaaS $10,000

3) If not billed at inception but invoiced monthly, the entries would reflect contract asset/liability and receivable timing — adjust accordingly.

Recognition schedule (summary):
- Day 0: Recognize $10,000 implementation revenue; defer $120,000 SaaS.
- Months 1–12: Recognize $10,000 SaaS revenue each month; at month 12 deferred SaaS balance = $0.

Variant: handling variable consideration (usage credits)
Example add‑on: contract includes up to $2,400 of usage credits in year (i.e., variable reduction in consideration). The entity expects customers will redeem $800 of credits on average.
- Step 1: Estimate variable consideration (expected value or most likely amount) = $800.
- Step 2: Apply the constraint: include in transaction price only the amount not likely to result in a significant revenue reversal. If historical patterns and current evidence support $800 and not likely to reverse materially, include $800; otherwise include a lower amount or $0.
- If included, adjust the transaction price allocated to the SaaS obligation: adjusted SaaS price = $120,000 − $800 = $119,200.
- Monthly SaaS recognition = $119,200 / 12 = $9,933.33 per month.
- Journal entries: initial deferred SaaS = $119,200 (instead of $120,000); monthly recognition Dr Deferred revenue $9,933.33; Cr Revenue $9,933.33. (Record actual credits when redeemed as a reduction of revenue/receipt or as a contra‑revenue per policy.)

Practical considerations and common pitfalls
- Contract modifications: treat as a separate contract or a modification of the existing one depending on new goods/services and pricing; document the analysis.
- Discounts and promotions: apply to all performance obligations proportionally unless an observable SSP indicates otherwise.
- Bundled goods/services: determine whether components are distinct; if not, account for combined as a single performance obligation.
- Renewal vs. new contracts: automatic renewals may be new contracts if terms/pricing materially change; watch for timing of revenue recognition and renewal consideration.
- Over time vs. point in time: evaluate transfer of control indicators (customer ability to benefit and direct control). Subscriptions are typically over time.
- Principal vs. agent: if you’re an agent, recognize net fee; evaluate control over the good/service being transferred.
- Costs to obtain/fulfill a contract: capitalize incremental costs of obtaining a contract (e.g., sales commissions) if expected to be recovered, and amortize consistent with revenue recognition; costs to fulfill may be capitalized if meet criteria.

Compliance tips and documentation best practices
- Evidence of transfer: retain contract, SOW, acceptance emails, implementation dates to support point‑in‑time recognition.
- Supporting estimates for variable consideration: maintain forecasting methodology, historical utilization, and sensitivity analysis.
- Disclosures: reconcile opening/closing contract balances, revenue recognized from performance obligations satisfied in previous periods, and judgements/estimates used (see ASC 606 / IFRS 15 disclosure requirements).
- Audit evidence: document your SSP methodology (market, adjusted market, expected cost plus margin, residual approach) and allocation calculations.
- When in doubt about significant judgments (e.g., constraining variable consideration, principal vs. agent), consult external auditors or legal counsel.

Short review checklist for a new customer contract (for finance teams)
1. Is there a signed, enforceable contract? If yes, capture effective date and term.
2. What are the promised goods/services? Are they distinct performance obligations?
3. What is the transaction price? Any variable consideration or significant financing components?
4. What are the SSPs? Document method and source.
5. Allocate transaction price and determine timing (over time vs. point in time).
6. Record initial journal entries (cash/AR, deferred revenue, revenue recognized at inception if any).
7. Document judgments: variable consideration estimates, contract modifications analysis, principal/agent conclusion.
8. File contract and supporting workpapers for disclosure/audit review.

Key takeaways and recommended next steps
1. Follow the five‑step model consistently; document each step and key judgments. (Consult ASC 606 / IFRS 15 guidance.)
2. Use SSPs to allocate transaction price; keep clear evidence for your SSP method. 
3. Treat variable consideration conservatively — include only amounts unlikely to reverse materially and document your methodology.
4. Build templates and a standard journal entry matrix for common contract types (SaaS, implementation, usage add‑ons) to reduce error.
5. Next steps: run a contract inventory, update sales/contract templates to capture needed evidence, and discuss judgment areas with your auditor.

Compliance and caution
This draft is educational and practical. It does not replace authoritative accounting advice—companies must apply ASC 606 / IFRS 15 to their facts and circumstances and consult auditors or counsel for judgment‑heavy items.

Sources / further reading
1. FASB ASC 606 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers (fasb.org).
2. IFRS 15 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers (ifrs.org).
3. PwC Revenue from Contracts with Customers (practical guide and illustrations).
4. Deloitte ASC 606 / IFRS 15 resources and illustrative examples.
5. EY Revenue recognition under ASC 606 / IFRS 15: guidance for accounting teams.
6. KPMG Revenue guides and implementation checklists.

(Include links to the above provider guidance and illustrative examples in final layout per editorial policy.)

Where requested, I can add a small formatted table for the recognition schedule and month‑by‑month journal entries.

Executive summary
This note explains how to apply ASC 606 / IFRS 15 to a simple, single-performance-obligation sale of goods. Using a numeric example (sale price $5,000; cost $3,000; delivery transfers control; no variable consideration, no financing component, collectability probable), the article walks through the five-step model, shows the required journal entries, illustrates income statement and balance-sheet effects, and gives a concise disclosure checklist and common pitfalls.

Background and the 5-step model (brief)
ASC 606 and IFRS 15 provide a single, principles-based framework for revenue from contracts with customers. The core is a five-step model:
1) Identify the contract(s) with the customer. 2) Identify the performance obligations in the contract. 3) Determine the transaction price. 4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations. 5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies the performance obligation(s) — i.e., when control transfers.

Definition of the “standard-revenue” scenario
We apply the model to a straightforward sale:
- Single contract to sell goods (one performance obligation). 
- Fixed consideration: price = $5,000. 
- Cost of goods sold (COGS) = $3,000. 
- Transfer of goods is at a point in time (delivery); control transfers on delivery. 
- No variable consideration, no significant financing component, no returns, collectability probable.

Apply the 5-step model to the example
Step 1 — Identify the contract
A contract exists when enforceable rights and obligations are present and collectability is probable. Here, the customer has agreed to purchase the goods for $5,000 and payment is probable — contract recognized.

Step 2 — Identify performance obligations
The contract obligates the seller to transfer a single distinct good to the customer. That is one performance obligation: delivery of the specified goods.

Step 3 — Determine the transaction price
The transaction price is the fixed amount of consideration expected: $5,000. No variable consideration, so no estimation or constraining is required. No financing component to adjust because payment timing does not give rise to significant financing.

Step 4 — Allocate the transaction price
Only one performance obligation exists, so the entire $5,000 is allocated to that obligation.

Step 5 — Recognize revenue when the obligation is satisfied
The obligation is satisfied at a point in time — when control of the goods transfers to the customer (normally on delivery). Therefore, recognize $5,000 revenue upon delivery/transfer of control.

Journal entries (examples)
A. Sale recognized at delivery (credit sale — cash collected later):
- Dr Accounts receivable 5,000
- Cr Revenue 5,000
- Dr Cost of goods sold 3,000
- Cr Inventory 3,000

B. Sale recognized at delivery (cash received at sale):
- Dr Cash 5,000
- Cr Revenue 5,000
- Dr Cost of goods sold 3,000
- Cr Inventory 3,000

C. Sales tax / withholding (if applicable)
Sales taxes collected on behalf of taxing authorities are not revenue. For example, if a 5% sales tax applied (not included in the $5,000 price), at sale:
- Dr Cash (or AR) 5,250
- Cr Revenue 5,000
- Cr Sales taxes payable 250
(Adjust the amounts depending on whether the $5,000 was stated inclusive or exclusive of tax.)

Presentation and financial-statement impact
Income statement (period of sale)
- Revenue: +$5,000
- Cost of goods sold: −$3,000
- Gross profit: +$2,000
Net income impact will reflect these amounts less operating expenses and tax.

Balance sheet (immediately after sale, if on credit)
- Assets: Accounts receivable +$5,000; Inventory −$3,000 (net decrease in current assets of $2,000). 
- Equity: Retained earnings will increase by net income after expense recognition (gross profit flows through to profit/loss when closed to equity).

Cash flow (operating activities)
- If cash collected at sale: operating cash inflow +$5,000. 
- If sale on credit: no immediate cash; cash inflow occurs when AR is collected. COGS reduces inventory — the physical outflow already occurred and is reflected in working capital movements.

Disclosure checklist (relevant to a standard case)
1. Revenue recognized from contracts with customers (primary sources and amounts) — disclose that revenue arises from sales of goods and the amount recognized. 
2. Significant judgments and estimates — disclose judgments about timing of transfer of control and assessment of collectability (here straightforward but should be noted). 
3. Remaining performance obligations if material — for simple immediate-delivery goods, remaining RPOs typically immaterial; disclose if material. 
4. Nature of goods/services and timing of transfer — point-in-time recognition; describe when control transfers. 
5. Disaggregation of revenue if material — e.g., by product line or geography if relevant to users.

Common pitfalls and notes
- Timing of transfer (control) vs. risks and rewards: don’t conflate legal title or shipping terms with control. Evaluate indicators of control under ASC 606/IFRS 15 (ability to direct use, obtain substantially all remaining benefits). 
- Principal vs. agent: if the seller is an agent (facilitator), only net fee is revenue. Here we assume the seller is principal and recognizes gross revenue. 
- Variable consideration / returns: not present in this example. If returns or discounts existed, estimate and constrain variable consideration per the standard. 
- Significant financing component: if payment terms materially finance the customer, adjust the transaction price for time value of money. Not present here. 
- Warranties: differentiate between assurance-type warranties (covered by a liability for expected costs) and service-type warranties (separate performance obligation).

References and further reading

- Deloitte: Revenue Recognition (ASC 606) Roadmap and IFRS 15 guides. 
- PwC: Revenue from Contracts with Customers (practical guides). 
- KPMG / AICPA technical summaries and illustrative examples.

Bottom line
For a standard single-good sale with fixed price and delivery transferring control, revenue is recognized at a point in time (on delivery) for the full transaction price. The accounting is straightforward: record revenue and remove inventory for COGS; present revenue, COGS and gross profit on the income statement; record cash or receivable on the balance sheet. Disclose the basis for recognizing revenue, any judgments (timing, collectability), and material remaining obligations.

2. Describe significant judgments (timing of transfer; collectability).

Lead
This short practical guide helps accountants, finance managers, and accounting students apply ASC 606 / IFRS 15 to common, non‑complex transactions: single goods, single services, and simple subscriptions. It focuses on the core principles and provides a worked numerical example, journal entries, and a compliance checklist.

Quick primer: core principle and the model
Core principle: recognize revenue when (or as) control of promised goods or services is transferred to a customer for an amount that reflects the consideration expected.

Four-step approach (concise):
1) Identify the contract with a customer.
2) Identify the performance obligation(s) — the distinct goods or services promised.
3) Determine the transaction price (consider discounts, refunds, immaterial variable consideration, and significant financing component).
4) Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations and recognize revenue when (or as) each obligation is satisfied (point‑in‑time or over time).

Applying the model to standard cases
Sale of a single good (point‑in‑time)
- Scenario: A customer buys a finished product for a fixed price with standard delivery and no returns beyond a short statutory right.
- Performance obligation: deliver the good.
- Recognition: point‑in‑time when control transfers (indicators include the company has a present right to payment, transfer of legal title, physical possession, customer acceptance, and significant risks and rewards). In many sale-of-goods situations, revenue is recognized on shipment or delivery depending on shipping terms and when control passes.
- Simple example: sell inventory for $1,000, FOB shipping point. Recognize revenue when goods are shipped (control transfers to buyer).

Single service delivered over time (when criteria met)
- Some services are satisfied over time (e.g., ongoing consulting, construction-type services) if any of the following are met: customer simultaneously receives and consumes benefits as the entity performs; entity’s performance creates or enhances an asset the customer controls; or the entity’s performance does not create an asset with an alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date.
- Recognition: measure progress (output methods like milestones or input methods like costs incurred) and recognize revenue over the service period.
- Simple example: a 6‑month retained advisory engagement invoiced upfront — recognize pro rata over 6 months if criteria are met.

Subscription for a single promise (monthly recognition)
- Scenario: customer pays for a single, continuous service (e.g., access to a software feature provided and consumed monthly).
- Performance obligation: continuous access/service; generally satisfied over time.
- Recognition: recognize revenue in the period the service is provided (e.g., monthly), converting cash received in advance to contract liability (deferred revenue) and releasing it each month.

Common simple issues and how to handle them
Discounts and refunds
- Apply the discount to the transaction price; if a contract includes a right of return, estimate expected returns and present as revenue less returns or adjust transaction price (use historical data when available).

Minor/immaterial variable consideration
- If variable consideration (rebates, volume discounts) is immaterial or can be reasonably estimated, include it in the transaction price using the expected value or most likely amount approach; reassess each reporting period. If immaterial, practical expedient allows ignoring it.

Contract modifications (not complex)
- Treat a simple modification that adds a distinct good/service as a separate contract. If not distinct, combine and treat as a modification to the original contract — typically adjust the remaining revenue to reflect the new combined transaction price.

Principal vs agent (simple reseller scenarios)
- Determine whether the entity controls the promised good/service before transfer to the customer. If it controls, recognize revenue gross (principal). If it arranges for another to provide the good/service and does not control it, recognize net (agent). Consider indicators: primary responsibility, inventory risk, price discretion.

Worked numerical example (assumptions flagged)
Example: Six‑month advisory contract, fixed price $12,000, invoiced and paid in full at contract start. The service is performed evenly over 6 months and qualifies for over‑time recognition.
Assumptions:
- No variable consideration, no significant financing component, no refunds, the service is distinct and consumed over time, and progress is measured on time elapsed (straight‑line).

Journal entries and timing:
At contract inception (cash received):
  Dr Cash 12,000
  Cr Contract liability (deferred revenue) 12,000

Monthly recognition (each month for 6 months):
  Dr Contract liability 2,000
  Cr Revenue — Advisory services 2,000

If costs incurred monthly (e.g., consultant payroll of $1,200/month):
  Dr Consulting expense 1,200
  Cr Cash/payables 1,200

If an adjustment were needed for a small customer refund in month 2 of $200 (expected and recognized):
  Dr Revenue (or Refund expense) 200
  Cr Cash/Payable 200

Compliance checklist and common pitfalls
- Have you identified each contract and its parties? (written, oral, implied) 
- Have you identified distinct performance obligations? (is each promise distinct?)
- Is your transaction price complete (include discounts, refunds, and material variable consideration)?
- Have you determined point‑in‑time vs over‑time based on control and the three over‑time criteria?
- Are you using a reasonable method to measure progress for over‑time recognition and documenting the rationale? 
- Are contract liabilities (deferred revenue) and receivables presented appropriately on the balance sheet? 
- Document estimates for returns or variable consideration and reassess each period.
- Common pitfalls: recognizing revenue on invoice date rather than when control transfers; failing to document why a service is over time; misclassifying principal vs agent in reseller arrangements.

Conclusion and further reading
For straightforward contracts, apply the four‑step approach consistently: identify the contract, identify performance obligations, determine and allocate the transaction price, and recognize revenue when control transfers or over time as appropriate. Keep concise documentation supporting judgments (control transfer, method of measuring progress, estimates). For complex scenarios (significant variable consideration, bundled long‑term contracts, complex modifications), consult full ASC 606 / IFRS 15 guidance or Big Four practice guides.

Further reading (authoritative sources):
- FASB ASC 606: Revenue from Contracts with Customers (FASB.org)
- IFRS 15: Revenue from Contracts with Customers (IFRS.org)
- PwC, Deloitte, EY, KPMG revenue recognition guides and roadmaps (search “ASC 606 guide” or “IFRS 15 guide” on each firm’s site) 

Keywords: revenue recognition ASC 606, IFRS 15, recognize revenue, point-in-time vs over time, revenue journal entries, standard revenue example

Note: This draft focuses on standard, non‑complex transactions; it intentionally excludes deep guidance on complex variable consideration, cost estimates for long‑term construction contracts, or highly negotiated multi‑element arrangements.

Title: Recognizing Revenue in a Standard Sale: Applying ASC 606/IFRS 15

Lead (2–3 sentences):
ASC 606/IFRS 15 replaced legacy revenue rules with a five-step model designed to align recognition with transfer of control. This practical explainer shows how to apply the model in the common, ‘‘standard’’ case — a single performance obligation, fixed price, control transfers at a point in time — with a concise numeric example and clear journal entries.

The five-step model (brief summary)
- 1) Identify the contract with a customer — a legally enforceable agreement that creates rights and obligations.[1]
- 2) Identify the performance obligations — promises in the contract to transfer goods or services (here: a single good).
- 3) Determine the transaction price — the amount the entity expects to be entitled to (here: fixed consideration).
- 4) Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations — for one obligation, the full price is allocated to that obligation.
- 5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies a performance obligation — for point-in-time cases, when control transfers to the customer.[1][2]

One-sentence linkage to the standard case: with a single, fixed-price performance obligation and control transferring at a point in time, revenue equals the fixed transaction price and is recognized at the delivery/acceptance moment.

Point-in-time recognition: how to tell when control transfers
Under ASC 606/IFRS 15, revenue is recognized when control of the good or service transfers. Indicators of transfer of control include (not exhaustive):
- Legal title to the asset passes to the customer.
- Physical possession transfers to the customer.
- The customer has significant risks and rewards of ownership.
- The customer has accepted the asset.
- The seller has a present right to payment for the asset.[1][2]

In the standard sale, these indicators typically align at delivery or customer acceptance; the entity recognizes revenue at that moment.

Measurement of the transaction price
In the standard scenario the transaction price is fixed consideration (no discounts, rebates, or contingent amounts). If variable consideration exists (estimations for returns, rebates, performance bonuses), it is estimated using either the expected value or most likely amount method and constrained if there is a risk of significant reversal of revenue.[1][2] For this article we assume fixed, collectible consideration.

Worked numeric example (facts and step-by-step application)
Facts
- Company A sells a machine to Customer B for $10,000 on credit.
- Single performance obligation: delivery of the machine.
- Control transfers on delivery (Customer B obtains physical possession and accepts the machine).
- No returns, no discounts, payment collectible.

Apply the five steps
1) Identify contract: Valid sales contract exists — enforceable rights and obligations.
2) Identify performance obligations: One obligation — transfer of the machine.
3) Determine transaction price: Fixed $10,000, collectible.
4) Allocate price: Single obligation receives the entire $10,000.
5) Recognize revenue: Control transfers at delivery; recognize entire $10,000 then.

Journal entries
- If sale on credit (recognize at point of delivery):
  - Dr Accounts Receivable $10,000
  - Cr Revenue $10,000
  - (Also record cost of goods sold and inventory removal as applicable)
    - Dr Cost of Goods Sold $X
    - Cr Inventory $X

- If cash received in advance (payment before control transfers):
  - At receipt of cash:
    - Dr Cash $10,000
    - Cr Contract Liability (Deferred Revenue) $10,000
  - When control transfers (on delivery):
    - Dr Contract Liability $10,000
    - Cr Revenue $10,000
  - (Record COGS and inventory movement at delivery as above.)

Required disclosures (concise list)
- Significant judgments about timing of satisfaction of performance obligations and indicators of control transfer.
- Description of performance obligations and significant payment terms.
- Contract balances: receivables, contract assets (if performance before invoicing), and contract liabilities (deferred revenue).
- Disaggregation of revenue by type, timing, and geography when material and relevant.[1][2]

Common pitfalls & compliance checklist (brief bullets)
- Misidentifying the point of control transfer vs relying solely on legal title (title may pass earlier or later than control).
- Ignoring significant financing components when payment terms are long (assess whether to adjust transaction price for time value of money).
- Failing to assess and constrain variable consideration (returns, rebates, performance bonuses).
- Misclassifying contract balances (contract asset vs receivable) and failing to disclose them clearly.
- Not documenting judgments and estimates (timing, collectibility, variable consideration methods).

Example variations (out-of-scope notes)
- Bundled goods/services (multiple performance obligations) require allocation of the transaction price to standalone selling prices — changes timing/amount of recognition.
- Discounts, expected returns, and consignment arrangements can introduce variable consideration or delay recognition.
- Principal versus agent considerations affect whether gross or net revenue is recognized.
These topics materially alter application of the five-step model and should be handled separately.

Conclusion (2–3 lines):
For the common fixed-price sale where control transfers at a point in time, ASC 606/IFRS 15 leads to straightforward recognition: revenue equals the agreed price and is recognized when control passes. Carefully document judgments about timing, payment terms, and any variable elements — and disclose contract balances and key judgments in the financial statements.

Authoritative sources and practical guides (selected)
- FASB ASC Topic 606 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) — FASB overview and resources: https://www.fasb.org/jsp/FASB/Page/SectionPage&cid=1176156246770 [FASB ASC 606]
- IFRS 15 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers: https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/ [IFRS 15]
- PwC — Revenue recognition and ASC 606/IFRS 15 resources: https://www.pwc.com/us/en/services/assurance/accounting-advisory/revenue-recognition.html [PwC guide]
- Deloitte, EY, KPMG practical guides and illustrative examples — see respective revenue recognition sections for application examples and implementation guidance.[3]

Footnotes:
[1] ASC 606/IFRS 15 five-step model and transfer of control concepts (see FASB and IASB standards).
[2] Indicators of control and guidance on variable consideration are discussed in ASC 606 and IFRS 15; estimates are constrained to avoid significant reversal.
[3] Big Four practical guides provide helpful interpretive assistance and illustrative examples (search Deloitte/Audit & Assurance revenue recognition; EY Revenue Recognition; KPMG Revenue).

Title: Practical Guide to Standard Revenue Recognition (ASC 606 / IFRS 15)

Why revenue recognition matters

Revenue drives profit, cash forecasting, tax positions, and investor decisions. Getting revenue recognition wrong can misstate earnings, mislead stakeholders, trigger restatements, and cause tax or regulatory issues. ASC 606 and IFRS 15 provide a consistent, principles-based framework to recognize revenue that reflects the transfer of promised goods or services to customers.

High-level overview: the 5-step model

Both ASC 606 and IFRS 15 use the same five-step model:

1) Identify the contract with a customer.
2) Identify the performance obligations (distinct goods or services).
3) Determine the transaction price (consider variable amounts, discounts, financing).
4) Allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations.
5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies each performance obligation.

(Authoritative sources: FASB ASC 606 overview: https://www.fasb.org; IFRS 15 summary: https://www.ifrs.org)

Key principles to remember

- Recognize revenue when control of a good or service transfers to the customer, not necessarily when cash is received.
- Variable consideration (returns, discounts, performance bonuses) is estimated and constrained per ASC 606/IFRS 15.
- Contracts with multiple distinct deliverables require allocation of the transaction price based on standalone selling prices.

Example 1 — One-time product sale with a right of return

Scenario and assumptions

- Company sells 100 electronic gadgets for $200 each (gross = $20,000).
- Customer has a 30-day right of return.
- Based on history, expected returns are 5 units (5%) and estimated refund cost is the sales price.
- The company uses the expected value method to estimate variable consideration (returns).
- Assume cost of goods sold (COGS) per unit = $120.

Step-by-step treatment

1) Recognize revenue net of expected returns. ASC 606 requires estimating variable consideration and constraining it.
2) Record the sale and a refund liability for estimated returns, and an asset for the right to recover inventory (expected returns inventory).

Journal entries (initial sale)

| Date | Account | Debit | Credit |
|------|---------|-------:|-------:|
| Sale day | Accounts receivable / Cash | 20,000 | |
| | Sales revenue | | 19,000* |
| | Refund liability | | 1,000* |

*Sales revenue credited net of estimated returns: 95 units x $200 = $19,000. Refund liability equals $1,000.

| Date | Account | Debit | Credit |
|------|---------|-------:|-------:|
| Sale day | Cost of goods sold | 12,000 | |
| | Inventory | | 12,000 |

COGS recorded for expected sold units: 95 units x $120 = $11,400. The remaining COGS for expected returns is treated through the returns inventory entry below.

Adjusting entries for expected returns (to reflect recoverable inventory)

| Date | Account | Debit | Credit |
|------|---------|-------:|-------:|
| Sale day | Refund liability | 1,000 | |
| | Inventory - expected returns (asset) | | 1,000 |

To record expected return of 5 units valued at $200 each (assumes no return-related cost; if return costs exist, include estimate).

When returns occur

- If a customer returns 1 unit: debit Refund liability $200, debit Inventory $120 (or reversal of estimated returns asset reduction), credit Cash/Accounts receivable $200, credit COGS reversal/Inventory accordingly.

Notes on estimation method

ASC 606 permits using either the expected value (probability-weighted) or most likely amount methods to estimate variable consideration. Use the method that better predicts the amount. Always apply the constraint to avoid significant reversals of revenue.

Example 2 — Subscription/service contract with distinct deliverables and multi-period performance

Scenario and assumptions

- A software vendor sells a 12-month subscription + one-time onboarding service for a bundled price of $12,000 payable upfront.
- Standalone prices: subscription $9,600 ($800 per month), onboarding $3,000.
- Onboarding is delivered at contract start (one-time); subscription access is provided over 12 months.
- Company follows ASC 606 allocation by relative standalone selling prices.

Step-by-step treatment

1) Identify performance obligations: onboarding (distinct) and 12 months of access (distinct series).
2) Determine transaction price: $12,000.
3) Allocate price using relative standalone selling prices:

Allocation table

| Deliverable | Standalone price | Allocation % | Allocated amount |
|-------------|------------------:|-------------:|-----------------:|
| Onboarding | 3,000 | 25% | 3,000 |
| Subscription (12 months) | 9,600 | 75% | 9,000 |
| Total | 12,600 | 100% | 12,000 |

Calculation: allocated amount = transaction price x (standalone price / total standalone prices). Here subscription allocated = $12,000 x (9,600/12,600) = $9,000.

Journal entries

Initial receipt (cash) and recognition of contract liability for deferred revenue:

| Date | Account | Debit | Credit |
|------|---------|-------:|-------:|
| Contract start | Cash | 12,000 | |
| | Deferred revenue (liability) | | 12,000 |

Recognize onboarding revenue at completion (immediate):

| Date | Account | Debit | Credit |
|------|---------|-------:|-------:|
| Onboarding complete | Deferred revenue | 3,000 | |
| | Revenue - onboarding | | 3,000 |

Recognize subscription revenue monthly (straight-line) over 12 months:

| Monthly | Deferred revenue | 750 | |
| | Subscription revenue | | 750 |

(Subscription allocated $9,000 / 12 = $750 per month.)

Notes on pattern of recognition

If the subscription performance obligation is satisfied over time (e.g., continuous access), recognize revenue over the period based on a systematic measure (time, usage). If control transfers at a point, recognize at that point.

Common pitfalls and how to avoid them

- Poor contract assessment: Missing optional renewals, embedded financing, or bundled goods leads to misstatements. Mitigate by using contract checklists and standardized templates.
- Mishandling variable consideration: Over- or under-weighting returns, rebates, or bonuses. Use historical data, choose an appropriate estimation method (expected value or most likely amount), and apply the constraint test.
- Incorrect allocation: Failing to use valid standalone selling prices. Avoid by documenting price lists, market evidence, and calculation workings.
- Timing errors: Recognizing revenue too early (before control transfers). Match recognition to when the customer obtains control.

Opening (why timing matters — ~120 words)
Accurately timing revenue recognition is a fundamental control for financial reporting. Revenue affects earnings, key performance indicators (gross margin, days sales outstanding), debt covenants, and investor perception. Mistimed revenue recognition is a frequent audit finding and a common source of restatements. For a straightforward sale of goods, applying the ASC 606 / IFRS 15 five-step model yields clear outcomes most of the time — but practical traps remain (shipping terms, bill-and-hold, consignment, variable consideration). This article explains the framework, walks through a numeric example, highlights indicators of transfer of control, and offers controls and disclosure guidance finance teams can apply immediately.

The five-step model (150–200 words)
Both ASC 606 and IFRS 15 use the same five-step revenue model:
1. Identify the contract with a customer — an agreement creating enforceable rights and obligations.
2. Identify the performance obligations — distinct promised goods or services.
3. Determine the transaction price — the amount the entity expects to be entitled to.
4. Allocate the transaction price to performance obligations — typically by relative standalone selling prices.
5. Recognize revenue when (or as) the performance obligation is satisfied — at a point in time or over time.

For the sale of finished goods where control transfers at delivery, there is usually a single performance obligation satisfied at a point in time. ASC 606 and IFRS 15 focus on transfer of control (not only transfer of risks and rewards). Indicators of transfer include physical possession, legal title, significant risks and rewards shifting, customer acceptance, and the seller’s right to payment.

Standard case scenario and facts (~60 words)
Manufacturer A sells 1,000 units to Distributor B at $100/unit = $100,000. Shipping term: FOB shipping point (control transfers when goods leave seller’s warehouse). Payment due in 30 days. Contract includes no returns, no installation or service, and no significant financing component.

Walkthrough applying the five steps (~350 words)
1. Identify the contract: A and B have a valid sales contract with enforceable payment terms and commercial substance. The contract meets ASC 606/IFRS 15 contract criteria.

2. Identify performance obligations: The contract promises delivery of 1,000 units of a standard product. There are no separate promised services or bundled elements. This is a single performance obligation: delivery of goods.

3. Determine the transaction price: The stated price is $100,000 (1,000 × $100). There is no variable consideration (no discounts, rebates, or returns), and no significant financing component (payment due in 30 days on a typical trade sale). Therefore the transaction price is $100,000.

4. Allocate the transaction price: Because there is only one performance obligation, all of the $100,000 is allocated to it.

5. Recognize revenue when performance obligation is satisfied: Under FOB shipping point, control transfers when goods leave Manufacturer A’s warehouse (the customer bears freight and risk). Using the indicators of control — physical possession transferred to carrier under terms that shift risk/reward, title commonly passes at shipment — revenue is recognized at shipment.

Numeric example (boxed example to include verbatim):
- Sale: 1,000 units × $100/unit = $100,000
- Shipping term: FOB shipping point (control transfers when goods leave seller's warehouse)
- Journal entries (at shipment):
  Debit Accounts Receivable $100,000; Credit Sales Revenue $100,000.
  Debit Cost of Goods Sold $60,000; Credit Inventory $60,000.
Note: If FOB destination, revenue recognized on delivery to customer (explain differences).

Practical journal entries explained: At the point of satisfaction (shipment for FOB shipping point), record the sale and related cost of goods sold. Record invoice issuance and set up an accounts receivable. If the company uses a separate billing step later, ensure revenue recognition aligns with transfer of control and not billing timing.

Controls and disclosures (150–200 words)
Controls
- Sales terms review: Require documented review and approval of key contract terms (shipping terms, return rights, acceptance clauses) before order confirmation.
- Shipment & fulfillment records: Maintain signed bills of lading, carrier receipts, or warehouse release notices that evidence transfer of goods.
- Cut-off procedures: Reconcile shipments near period end to revenue recorded in the period; test a sample of pre- and post-period shipments.
- Invoicing timing: Ensure invoicing policies don’t drive recognition (revenue should reflect control transfer, not invoice date).
- Returns and allowances: Maintain and review estimates for sales returns and record allowances when probable and estimable.

Disclosures
- Revenue recognition policy: Disclose when performance obligations are satisfied (point in time vs. over time) and key judgments (shipping terms, variable consideration).
- Accounts receivable and credit risk: Provide aging and allowance policies, and any significant contract balances such as contract assets/liabilities.
- Significant judgments and estimates: Explain judgments about transfer of control, returns, and significant financing components.

Pitfalls & common variations (150–200 words)
- Consignment vs. sale: Under consignment, the seller retains control until the consignee sells to end customers. Revenue is not recognized at shipment to a consignee. Look for indicators: right to recall, inventory recorded by consignor.
- Bill-and-hold: Revenue recognition before physical transfer is allowed only if strict criteria are met (e.g., substantive reason for bill-and-hold, goods identified and ready for transfer, seller cannot use goods). Many bill-and-hold arrangements fail the criteria.
- Variable consideration: Discounts, rebates, returns, and performance bonuses create variable consideration. Apply the constraint (only include amounts not probable to reverse materially) when estimating transaction price.
- Significant financing component: Long payment terms may indicate a financing element requiring separation of implicit interest; short, customary trade terms generally do not.
- Warranties vs. assurance-type: Distinguish between assurance warranties (no separate revenue) and service or extended warranties that are separate performance obligations.
- Bundled goods/services: When goods are bundled with installation or ongoing service, assess whether separate performance obligations exist and allocate the price accordingly.

Conclusion & practical checklist (~70 words)
Accurate revenue timing for a standard sale of goods depends on applying the five-step model and documenting the transfer of control. Below is a practical checklist finance teams can use at month-end.

5-item practical checklist
1. Confirm shipping terms and supporting shipping documents (BOL/carrier receipts).
2. Match shipments to sales orders and invoices for proper cut-off.
3. Verify no outstanding conditions (acceptance clauses, returns, consignment terms).
4. Review whether any variable consideration or significant financing exists.
5. Document judgments (policy disclosure) and retain audit trail for each material sale.

Assumptions
- The example assumes no returns, no installation or other promised services, and no significant financing component.

Five-step model overview (approx. 120 words)
Apply these five steps to every customer contract per ASC 606 / IFRS 15:
1) Identify the contract with a customer. 2) Identify the performance obligation(s). 3) Determine the transaction price. 4) Allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation. 5) Recognize revenue when (or as) the entity satisfies the performance obligation (transfer of control).
For a single-good sale with fixed price and point-in-time transfer, the application is typically direct: one contract, one performance obligation, full price allocated to that obligation, and revenue recognized when control transfers (usually on shipment or delivery depending on terms).

Step-by-step applied example (approx. 500 words)
Scenario (compact): Company A sells 100 widgets to Customer B at $50 each. Total invoice = $5,000. Shipping terms: FOB shipping point; Company A invoices on shipment; payment due in 30 days. Customer has a 30-day return window. Historical return rate = 2% (insignificant to customer acceptance). No other discounts, variable consideration, or significant financing components.

1) Identify the contract: Signed purchase order or sales agreement plus evidence of commercial substance and enforceable rights/obligations. Here a confirmed sale with invoice on shipment meets the contract criteria (ASC 606/IFRS 15 require that collectibility be probable). Cite: ASC 606 / IFRS 15 overview.[1][2]

2) Identify performance obligations: The contract promises delivery of widgets only; that is one distinct performance obligation satisfying criteria for separability. No additional goods or services are promised.

3) Determine the transaction price: Contract price is $5,000. Consider potential adjustments — here an expected return rate of 2% implies variable consideration; because it is estimable and constrained only to the extent it is probable that a significant reversal will not occur, recognize an expected returns liability (refund liability) and an asset for expected returns inventory when appropriate.[1]

4) Allocate to performance obligations: Single performance obligation receives full transaction price (subject to adjustment for expected returns).

5) Recognize revenue when control transfers: FOB shipping point means control transfers on shipment. Revenue is therefore recognized on shipment (assuming collectibility is probable and other criteria met).

Calculations (simple bullet list):
- Unit price × quantity = 50 × 100 = 5,000
- Estimated returns (2%) = 0.02 × 5,000 = 100
- Recognized revenue at shipment (gross) = 5,000, with an offsetting refund liability of 100 for expected returns

Journal entries (compact, illustrative):
1) On shipment (recognize sale and receivable):
   Dr Accounts Receivable 5,000
   Cr Revenue 5,000

2) Record expected returns reserve at time of sale (estimate 2%):
   Dr Sales Returns and Allowances (contra-revenue) 100
   Cr Refund Liability 100
   (Alternatively, entities can present refund liability and an asset for returned goods; adjust based on policy and presentation guidance.)

3) When returns occur (example: customer returns goods worth $60):
   Dr Refund Liability 60
   Cr Accounts Receivable / Cash 60
   Dr Inventory — Recoverable from Returns 60 (if entity records an asset for expected returns)
   Cr Cost of Goods Sold 60 (to reverse cost previously recognized as appropriate)

Notes on presentation: Many entities present revenue net of returns using contra accounts; others present refund liabilities separately and recognize an asset for expected returns. Follow your presentation policy and disclose judgments about estimates and their measurement.

Document the following to support point-in-time recognition:
- Signed purchase order or sales contract and invoice (shows contract terms and price). 
- Shipping documents and carrier bills of lading (evidence of transfer under FOB shipping point). 
- Sales terms and customer payment terms (show no significant financing component). 
- Return policy and historical return statistics (support the estimate for expected returns). 
- Internal approval of collectibility assessments and credit checks.

3) Mixed case (product + ongoing service):
- Scenario: Company sells hardware with a 2-year maintenance contract.

Quick summary
This article explains the ASC 606 / IFRS 15 five-step model with a practical SaaS example, shows how to allocate a bundled contract using relative standalone selling prices, and provides month-end checklist items for audit readiness.

The five-step model in one paragraph
The core framework is the five-step model that all entities use to account for revenue from contracts with customers: (1) identify the contract with a customer; (2) identify the performance obligations in the contract; (3) determine the transaction price; (4) allocate the transaction price to the performance obligations; and (5) recognize revenue when or as the performance obligations are satisfied (FASB ASC 606 guidance; IFRS 15 guidance) (https://asc.fasb.org/, https://www.ifrs.org/issued-standards/list-of-standards/ifrs-15-revenue-from-contracts-with-customers/).

Step 1 and Step 2: identify the contract and the performance obligations
- Identify the contract: a contract is an agreement between two parties that creates enforceable rights and obligations. It may be written, oral, or implied by customary business practices (ASC 606). Common contract boundaries include termination rights, renewal options, and payment terms. (See FASB ASC 606 guidance.)
- Identify performance obligations: a performance obligation is a promise to transfer a distinct good or service to the customer. Two tests determine distinctness: (a) the customer can benefit from the good or service on its own or together with other readily available resources (standalone utility), and (b) the promise is separately identifiable from other promises in the contract. Practical indicators that a promise is not separately identifiable include significant integration, modification, or interdependence of promised goods and services (ASC 606 / IFRS 15).
- Examples in SaaS: software subscription access, implementation services, customization, and training are often separate promises. Implementation and training are frequently distinct if they are sold separately and the customer can benefit from them independently.

Step 3: determine the transaction price
- The transaction price is the amount of consideration the entity expects in exchange for transferring goods or services. Consider variable consideration, the constraint on variable amounts, and any significant financing component. Variable consideration includes discounts, refunds, credits, performance bonuses, rebates, and similar items. Use either expected value or most likely amount methods, and apply a constraint if there is significant uncertainty that the estimate will not reverse (ASC 606 / IFRS 15 guidance).
- Practical note: for contracts with upfront payment for future services, consider whether the timing of payment indicates a significant financing component. If the payment and transfer timings are within the entitys customary credit period, a financing component is unlikely.

Step 4: allocate the transaction price to performance obligations
- Allocation principle: allocate the transaction price to each performance obligation based on its relative standalone selling price (SSP). Use observable prices when available. When observable SSPs are not available, determine SSP using one of three approaches: adjusted market assessment, expected cost plus margin, or residual approach (residual only when SSPs for one or more performance obligations are highly variable or uncertain and observable SSPs exist for other obligations).
- Methods summary and when to use them:
  - Observable selling price: preferred when the entity sells the item separately in similar circumstances.
  - Adjusted market assessment: use if an entity can estimate what customers would pay in the market by comparing competitor prices or market data.
  - Expected cost plus margin: use when costs and an appropriate margin can be estimated reliably, common for bespoke services.
  - Residual approach: use rarely, only where other SSPs are available and certain obligations have highly variable prices.

Worked example: SaaS subscription with implementation and training
Facts (use these exact facts): Company A sells a 12-month cloud software subscription plus a one-time implementation service and two days of training under a single contract. Total contract price: **120,000** (paid upfront). Observable standalone selling prices from other contracts: subscription (12 months) = **96,000**; implementation = **18,000**; 2 days training = **6,000**. Implementation completed at contract start; training provided in month 1; subscription delivered evenly over 12 months.

Step-by-step allocation math
1. Sum of standalone selling prices: **96,000 + 18,000 + 6,000 = 120,000**.
2. Allocation ratios:
   - Subscription: 96,000 / 120,000 = 0.80
   - Implementation: 18,000 / 120,000 = 0.15
   - Training: 6,000 / 120,000 = 0.05
3. Allocated amounts (relative SSP method):
   - Subscription: **96,000**
   - Implementation: **18,000**
   - Training: **6,000**

Recognition timing and journal entries
- At contract inception, cash is received and wholly deferred until the entity satisfies obligations (subject to any billing/contract specifics).
  - On receipt of cash:
    Dr Cash **120,000**
    Cr Deferred revenue (contract liability) **120,000**
- Implementation recognized at point in time when completed (contract start):
    Dr Deferred revenue **18,000**
    Cr Revenue - implementation services **18,000**
- Training recognized at point in time when delivered (month 1):
    Dr Deferred revenue **6,000**
    Cr Revenue - training services **6,000**
- Subscription recognized over time ratably (even delivery over 12 months): monthly recognition = **96,000 / 12 = 8,000** per month.
  - Monthly journal entry (months 1 through 12):
    Dr Deferred revenue **8,000**
    Cr Revenue - subscription **8,000**
- Practical check: total recognized at the end of 12 months equals **18,000 + 6,000 + (8,000 x 12 = 96,000) = 120,000**.

Step 5: recognize revenue — over time vs point in time
- Over time recognition applies when any of these criteria are met: (a) the customer simultaneously receives and consumes the benefits as the entity performs, (b) the entitys performance creates or enhances an asset controlled by the customer, or (c) the entitys performance does not create an asset with an alternative use and the entity has an enforceable right to payment for performance completed to date. Otherwise, revenue is recognized at a point in time when control transfers (ASC 606 / IFRS 15).
- In SaaS, subscriptions are typically over time because access is provided continuously and the customer receives benefits continuously. Implementation and training are frequently point in time when completed or delivered.
- Journal-entry level descriptions were shown in the worked example above.

Common pitfalls and practical tips
- Discount allocation: when a contract contains a discount that spans multiple obligations, allocate the discount proportionally to SSPs unless a specific observable pattern indicates another method is more appropriate.
- Contract modifications: treat modifications as a separate contract or an amendment based on whether additional goods/services are distinct and whether the price increases by an amount reflecting standalone prices (ASC 606 guidance). Document the assessment.
- Variable consideration: apply the expected value or most likely amount method and apply the constraint to avoid recognizing revenue that is likely to reverse.
- Principal versus agent: determine whether the entity controls the good or service before transfer to the customer. If the entity controls the specified good or service, recognize revenue on a gross basis; if it is acting as an agent, recognize net.
- Combining contracts: combine contracts if they are negotiated as a package with one commercial objective, or if rights and payment terms are interrelated. Ensure consistent treatment.

Infographic concept and caption text
- Concept: five-step flowchart with rectangles for each step connected left to right; under each rectangle a one-line prompt.
- Caption text to include with the infographic: "Five-step revenue recognition flowchart: 1 Identify contract, 2 Identify performance obligations, 3 Determine transaction price, 4 Allocate price to SSPs, 5 Recognize as obligations are satisfied. Use observable SSPs first; apply the constraint for variable consideration." 

Checklist for month-end close and audit readiness (7 items)
1. Verify contract scope and ensure all contract modifications are recorded and assessed.
2. Confirm performance obligations and document distinctness tests with evidence of standalone sales or indicators.
3. Reconcile transaction price components and test variable consideration estimates and constraints.
4. Confirm SSPs used for allocation; document method and supporting data (observable prices, market analysis, cost plus, or residual justification).
5. Reconcile deferred revenue ledger to contract schedules and cash receipts; test cutoffs around month end.
6. Review revenue recognition timing for over time vs point in time and ensure journal entries match delivery patterns.
7. Prepare clear disclosures notes for revenue policies, significant judgments, remaining performance obligation roll‑forwards, and contract balances.

- FASB ASC Topic 606 — Revenue from Contracts with Customers. FASB ASC online resource. https://asc.fasb.org/
